gratuitous

gruh-TOO-uh-tus -- from Latin gratuitus, 'free, given as a favor,' from gratia, 'favor, kindness': something gratuitous is given without being asked for. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Gratuitous is uncalled for and unwarranted.

The critic complained that the play's extra twenty minutes of unrelated dance numbers felt entirely gratuitous.

Example

The coach added a gratuitous, unannounced extra lap around the field purely to make an example of the one player who had arrived two minutes late.

Gratuitous describes something added without real justification, often just to make a point or for effect -- an extra lap that punishes the whole team for one late arrival serves no real training purpose beyond making an example.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

excessive: Excessive means too much of something that may be perfectly fine in smaller amounts -- salt, homework, screen time. Gratuitous attacks the justification instead of the quantity: even one gratuitous insult is one too many, because nothing in the situation called for it at all.

superfluous: Superfluous describes harmless extra -- a tenth pencil, a second umbrella -- left over beyond what is needed, with no blame attached. Gratuitous is an accusation: the extra thing was added deliberately and without justification, often to shock or wound. A superfluous scene pads a film; a gratuitous one offends.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

justified: shown to be right or reasonable

necessary: required; needed

Where it sits · how little justification it has

needless → gratuitous → unwarranted

needless vs. gratuitous: Needless is a plain, everyday word for anything unnecessary, while gratuitous adds a sharper criticism that something was added deliberately and inappropriately.

unwarranted vs. gratuitous: Unwarranted goes a step further than gratuitous by emphasizing that something wasn't just unnecessary but actively lacked any real justification.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — gratuit: given freely, as a favor (from Latin gratuitus, built on gratus 'pleasing, thankful' -- the same root as gratitude, and as gratuity, a tip given freely)

Suffix — -ous: full of, having the quality of (Latin -osus)

Put it together: Gratuit ('given freely, as a favor', from Latin gratuitus, built on gratus 'pleasing, thankful') + -ous ('full of') spell gratuitous: something gratuitous was originally just 'given for free' -- the same root behind gratitude and gratuity.

Use the root in a new word: gratitude: She wrote a heartfelt note of gratitude to the nurse who had cared for her father.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Gratuitous is almost always a criticism, suggesting something -- often violence, detail, or cruelty -- went further than the situation actually called for.
